Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. Issues.Title: Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs
Issues.Body:
I'm completely perplexed.

I created a .Net Standard 2.0 library project.

I explicity added an AssemblyInfo.cs file, we need this because we use this utility to "stamp" our assemblies when we build them:

https://github.com/ygoe/NetRevisionTool

That utility is run as a pre/post build event and temporarily replaces placeholders in the AssemblyInformationalVersion attribute with runtime values (like repo folder name, commit ID, branch etc etc).

The completed assembly then has this info "burned" into it as we go forward.

.Net Standard is not working with this.

1. It seems to populatethe Package Version (in the project's Package section) with whatever we put into AssemblyInfo.cs for AssemblyInformationalVersion.
2. The version of the generated nuget package is always set as 1.0.0.

This is just mind blowing, is there no way we can do this seemingly simple operation any more if adopt .Net Standard?

Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions" (#1777)

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1" (#1787)

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions" (#1786)

Issues.Title: linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem
Issues.Body:
Hello,

I am currently using .NET core 2.2.x and EF Core. 2.2.6. I have a function that returns a List<Animal> from the database with no issue. It returns 11 results. However, when I try to use `.Where(p => p.DeletedAt.GetValueOrDefault(DateTime.Now) => DateTime.Now).ToList()`, it still should return 11 results, however it returns 0. I also eliminated the possibility that there is something wrong with my where clause (logic) because it works perfectly on 4.6.1 EF Core 2.2.6. Furthermore, I confirmed that it is only where I am comparing a nullable type using that function and I am guessing that I missed a thread someone opened on this issue. I am aware .NET core 2.2 is not LTS. I also thought this goes here because it's not AFAIK, an EF core issue but rather an Ienumerable/Linq issue.

Update: As it turns out your notion of `DateTime.Now` getting evaluated twice is true. To rectify that, I will now be using `DateTime.Now.Date`. This is odd because this exact code works on 4.6.1. You're probably right. SMH. Thank you @GrabYourPitchforks! You may now close.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem" (#1792)

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Best Regards, Raphael --- ### Original Comments #### Raphael Affolter on 1/20/2020, 04:03 AM:

I forgot to mention: .Net Framework 4.6.1

#### Feedback Bot on 1/20/2020, 06:51 PM:

We have directed your feedback to the appropriate engineering team for further evaluation. The team will review the feedback and notify you about the next steps.

Because we print a lot, we really suffer from this performance penalty.

Also reading PaperSizes and PaperSources from the printer settings is slow caused by the same problem.

Could you please inform me about a possible fix?

Best Regards,

Raphael

FastDeviceCapabilities.

Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF" (#1776)

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Title: Fix Razor using directive sorting in the presence of aliases and statics
Issues.Body:
More work found while doing using aliases, and extracted here to try to keep that PR size down.

We already had sort usings functionality in Razor, it just didn't get alias coverage, and I discovered the same about static usings. This broadly matches Roslyn's behaviour, though we avoid parsing the directives and just do string comparisons, so there are edges that will differ. They're pretty niche.

This also deliberately doesn't cover pathological cases such as `using static/* foo*/Goo` or `using static /* = */ Foo`, again to avoid re-parsing C#.

Issues.Title: Preserve speculative binder when checking local Main signatures
Issues.Body:
Speculative binding of a top-level local function named `Main` returning `Task` or `Task<T>` throws `KeyNotFoundException` because entry-point signature checking requests a compilation binder for speculative syntax.

**Implementation is pending plan approval; no code changes have been made.**

- **Proposed fix:** Thread an optional binder through `HasEntryPointSignature` and `ReturnsAwaitableToVoidOrInt`, supplying the local function’s binder.
- **Proposed regression coverage:** Exercise speculative return-type binding for async and non-async functions under executable and library output.

Issues.Title: Record individual analyzer refs from framework/sdk
Issues.Body:
Fixes https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-dotnettools/issues/3658

Reloading an .lscache currently restores every C# analyzer from a referenced framework pack, including analyzers MSBuild removed. This can cause duplicate logging generators and enable off-by-default generators in the editor even when command-line builds are clean.

Preserve MSBuild’s actual analyzer selection while keeping caches compact and environment-independent:

- Add frameworkAnalyzerReferences for selected targeting-pack analyzers. 
- Replace sdkAnalyzerPacks with sdkAnalyzerPackageReferences for selected analyzers from SDK-known NuGet packages. 
- Store compressed, pack-relative paths without installation roots or package versions, and load only the recorded files. 
- Keep selections in their target-framework slices so common entries cannot bind to the wrong pack version. 
- Leave metadata-reference pack expansion unchanged. 
- Bump the cache format to version 3 so older readers cannot silently misinterpret the new selection semantics. Version 2 caches require regeneration. 
 ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86244)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Record individual analyzer refs from framework/sdk" (#86244)

Issues.Title: Fix Razor rename issue with using aliases
Issues.Body:
Found while working on adding proper support for using aliases to Razor, and thought it was worth splitting out to a separate PR.

Sonic gave us two generated C# documents per Razor document, a "decl" and "impl" document, and each one gets all of the using directives emitted to it. Using aliases in C# are document local, however, so when renaming one, Roslyn only (correctly) renamed things in one of the two documents. This meant that there would be compile errors in the result, either from one document still using the old alias, or from the using directive edit being dropped because it was assumed that edits to using directives would be equivalent in both documents.

The solution, and what this PR does, is twofold: 1, detect a rename of an alias, and collect rename edits from both documents, and 2, combine and map edits from both documents to Razor _before_ processing using directives.

Issues.Title: FBA: Fix unreliable DTBs of `#:ref` target projects
Issues.Body:
Fixes an issue reported on Teams by @DamianEdwards

This might have been a regression introduced by #84139, though I need to double check.

https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/65d349930a64a00fb6588bd0dc17e41f05993781/src/Workspaces/MSBuild/BuildHost/Build/ProjectBuildManager.cs#L226
 
It looks like because we are not creating an intermediate `MSB.Evaluation.Project`, but instead going straight to `ProjectInstance`, the full `projectRootElement` does not get explicitly retained in the `_projectCollection`.
 
Then here: https://github.com/dotnet/msbuild/blob/4f3669e6c4d4f1aaaf2bd52eed8337a2c0f9fe52/src/Build/Evaluation/ProjectRootElementCache.cs#L290

I believe what is happening is: msbuild might need the `projectRootElement` holding the referent project of the `#:ref` later, in order to load it. But depending on whether it was in cache (see `_strongCache`/`_weakCache` fields), it might end up going to disk to look for it. It's an in-memory project though, so going to disk won't work, and will result in the failure Damian observed. The failure is nondeterministic and seems more likely to occur when lots of different projects are being loaded.

I fixed this by explicitly creating an `Evaluation.Project` and loading that into the `_projectCollection`. This has the effect of explicitly retaining the `projectRootElement`.

One issue here is I don't think these get unloaded. Some investigation is needed to find the appropriate point at which to unload, I believe it is not the Dispose method of the containing type where the impl change was made.

But, it doesn't look like our MSBuildHost dealt with unloading at all until recently, so perhaps we can live without unloading of in-memory projects for the short term.
 
I think in the medium/long term we should talk to msbuild about our practice of building projects which don't exist on disk. We should set things up so it's easier to verify things are correct "by construction".

---

I was able to verify that the new test failed reliably before the change and passes afterwards.

I opted not to add an explicitly FBA/end-to-end test as exposing the ability to clear the cache in the remote msbuild host at the right time to repro the bug seemed excessively difficult. Instead I am just testing in MSBuildHost tests "locally".

Issues.Title: VB.NET: CInt(Math.Truncate(Double)) returns 22 instead of 21 inside an Async method
Issues.Body:
# VB.NET: `CInt(Math.Truncate(Double))` returns 22 instead of 21 inside an Async method

## Description

The expression `CInt(Math.Truncate(x))` produces different results depending on whether it is executed inside a regular method or an `Async` method.

When `x` is `21.5R`, the expression should return `21`, because `Math.Truncate` returns `21.0`. However, inside an `Async` method, `CInt(Math.Truncate(x))` returns `22`.

This behavior is reproducible in a .NET 10 console application and a clean WPF application. It also occurs in my existing WPF application, BloyectDesk.

## Minimal reproduction

```vb
Imports System
Imports System.Threading.Tasks

Module Program

    Sub Main(args As String())

        Console.WriteLine("Synchronous method:")
        TestConversions()

        Console.WriteLine()
        MainAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult()

        Console.ReadKey()

    End Sub

    Sub TestConversions()

        Dim x As Double = 21.5R

        Dim a As Integer = CInt(Math.Truncate(x))
        Dim b As Integer = CInt(Math.Truncate(CDbl(x)))
        Dim c As Integer = CInt(Math.Truncate(21.5R))
        Dim d As Integer = Convert.ToInt32(Math.Truncate(x))

        Console.WriteLine($"Truncate: {Math.Truncate(x)}")
        Console.WriteLine($"a = {a}")
        Console.WriteLine($"b = {b}")
        Console.WriteLine($"c = {c}")
        Console.WriteLine($"d = {d}")

    End Sub

    Async Function MainAsync() As Task

        Console.WriteLine("Async method:")

        Dim x As Double = 21.5R

        Dim a As Integer = CInt(Math.Truncate(x))
        Dim b As Integer = CInt(Math.Truncate(CDbl(x)))
        Dim c As Integer = CInt(Math.Truncate(21.5R))
        Dim d As Integer = Convert.ToInt32(Math.Truncate(x))

        Console.WriteLine($"Truncate: {Math.Truncate(x)}")
        Console.WriteLine($"a = {a}")
        Console.WriteLine($"b = {b}")
        Console.WriteLine($"c = {c}")
        Console.WriteLine($"d = {d}")

        Await Task.CompletedTask

    End Function

End Module
```

## Actual behavior

Synchronous method:

```text
Truncate: 21
a = 21
b = 21
c = 21
d = 21
```

Async method:

```text
Truncate: 21
a = 22
b = 22
c = 22
d = 21
```

## Expected behavior

Both methods should produce the same results:

```text
Truncate: 21
a = 21
b = 21
c = 21
d = 21
```

`Math.Truncate(21.5R)` returns `21.0`. Converting that value to `Integer` should produce `21`, regardless of whether the expression is inside an asynchronous method.

## Additional observations

- The behavior reproduces in a .NET 10 console application.
- It also reproduces in a clean WPF application targeting .NET 10 for Windows.
- The same expressions behave correctly in a synchronous method.
- `Convert.ToInt32(Math.Truncate(x))` consistently returns `21`.
- The issue appears to be associated with the VB.NET compiler's handling of `CInt(Math.Truncate(...))` inside an `Async` method.

I have not yet confirmed whether this is related to a particular compiler version or optimization setting.

## Environment

- Target framework: .NET 10
- Language: Visual Basic .NET
- Operating system: Windows
- IDE: Visual Studio (exact version to be provided)
- VB compiler version: To be confirmed

Could this be a compiler bug in the handling or optimization of `CInt(Math.Truncate(...))` inside asynchronous methods?

Issues.Title: Hot reload crashes with "An item with the same key has already been added. Key: 0" editing an async method with captures and an await in catch/finally
Issues.Body:
## Description

Editing a method under `dotnet watch` crashes the watcher with an `ArgumentException` from
`DefinitionMap.MakeLambdaAndClosureMapFromMetadata` when the method:

1. is `async`,
2. has lambdas that capture **both** a parameter and a local declared in the method body, and
3. contains an `await` inside a `catch` or `finally` block.

Removing any one of the three makes the problem go away.

The baseline PDB already has the bad data. The method's `EncLambdaAndClosureMap` custom debug
information (`A643004C-0240-496F-A783-30D64F4979DE`) holds **two closures with syntax offset 0**:
the parameter closure and the body-scope closure, which become separate scopes once the
await-in-catch/finally rewrite runs. `MakeLambdaAndClosureMapFromMetadata` builds a dictionary keyed
on `SyntaxOffset` via `ToImmutableSegmentedDictionary`, so it throws on the duplicate.

`dotnet watch` then exits, killing the app, instead of falling back to a restart.

## Repro

`Repro1.csproj`
```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup><OutputType>Exe</OutputType><TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework><ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings></PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

`Program.cs`
```csharp
while (true) { await C.P1(1); await Task.Delay(1000); }
static class C
{
    static Task<bool> F(Func<int, bool> f) => Task.FromResult(f(1));
    public static async Task P1(int p)
    {
        await F(x => x == p);   // lambda captures a parameter
        var l = 1;
        await F(x => x == l);   // lambda captures a local
        Console.WriteLine("v1");
        try { await Task.Yield(); } catch (Exception) { await Task.Yield(); }   // await in catch (finally behaves the same)
    }
}
```

1. `dotnet watch run`
2. Change `"v1"` to `"v2"` and save.

### Expected
The change is applied, or `dotnet watch` reports a rude edit and restarts.

### Actual
```
dotnet watch ❌ An unexpected error occurred: System.ArgumentException: An item with the same key has already been added. Key: 0
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Collections.Internal.ThrowHelper.ThrowAddingDuplicateWithKeyArgumentException[T](T key)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Collections.SegmentedDictionary`2.TryInsert(TKey key, TValue value, InsertionBehavior behavior)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Collections.ImmutableSegmentedDictionary`2.ValueBuilder.AddRange(IEnumerable`1 items)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Collections.ImmutableSegmentedDictionary`2.AddRange(IEnumerable`1 pairs)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Collections.ImmutableSegmentedDictionary.ToImmutableSegmentedDictionary[TSource,TKey,TValue](...)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Emit.DefinitionMap.MakeLambdaAndClosureMapFromMetadata(EditAndContinueMethodDebugInformation debugInfo, IMethodSymbolInternal method, DebugId methodId, IReadOnlyDictionary`2& lambdaMap, IReadOnlyDictionary`2& closureMap)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Emit.DefinitionMap.TryCreateVariableSlotAllocator(...)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.MethodCompiler.LowerBodyOrInitializer(...)
   ...
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Emit.EmitHelpers.EmitDifference(...)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.EditAndContinue.EditSession.EmitSolutionUpdateAsync(...)
   at Microsoft.DotNet.Watch.CompilationHandler.HandleManagedCodeChangesAsync(...)
```

## Closure map variants (from the baseline PDB)

| Method shape | Closure syntax offsets |
|---|---|
| captures param + local, `await` in `catch` | `[0, 0]` ❌ |
| captures param + local, `await` in `finally` | `[0, 0]` ❌ |
| captures param + local (one lambda), `await` in `catch` | `[0, 0]` ❌ |
| captures param + local, no `await` in `catch` | `[0]` ✅ |
| captures two locals (no param), `await` in `catch` | `[0]` ✅ |
| captures param only, `await` in `catch` | `[0]` ✅ |

## Impact

This is a common shape in real code: transactional service methods that query by a parameter, capture
locals in later lambdas, and `await transaction.RollbackAsync()` in a `catch`. 23 methods in our
application's main service assembly have the duplicate, and every edit to any of them kills
`dotnet watch`.

## Environment

- Reproduced on SDK **10.0.102** and **10.0.403** (macOS arm64). The 11.0.100-rc.3 compiler emits the
  same duplicate offsets in the PDB. I didn't get its `dotnet watch` to run, so the crash itself isn't
  confirmed there.
- `dotnet watch run` (CLI)

## Related

Another user reported the same `Key: 0` stack on SDK 10.0.101 in a comment on dotnet/sdk#45455, with
no repro. That issue was about a different, already-fixed crash.

Issues.Title: Preserve existing newlines in unchanged complex trivia
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Preserve existing newline sequences in complex-trivia whitespace when the formatter would otherwise change only the newline encoding.

Tab-indented comments take the complex-trivia formatting path even when correctly formatted. That path regenerates whitespace using the configured newline, which defaults to the platform newline. On Windows this can introduce CRLF into an otherwise LF file and produce IDE0055 diagnostics without any indentation change.

The shared trivia formatter now preserves original non-elastic whitespace when its spacing and line structure already match the desired output, ignoring only EOL encoding. Both text-change and syntax-trivia outputs use this path. Genuine indentation, spacing, trailing-whitespace, and line-count changes, as well as elastic whitespace, continue to use the preferred newline.

This follows the existing ordinary-whitespace behavior: `end_of_line` controls generated or rebuilt whitespace, rather than requiring the core formatter to normalize every existing newline.

Related: dotnet/vscode-csharp#6817.

## Tests

- Added permanent C# coverage for matching and opposite LF/CRLF preferences, default options, tabs/spaces, mixed line endings, genuine corrections, inserted newlines with and without comments, and elastic whitespace.
- Added VB regression coverage for matching and opposite LF/CRLF preferences.
- Verified the newline-preservation regressions fail against the unfixed implementation and pass with the fix. Tests cover text-change and syntax-trivia output.
- C# workspace formatting tests: 730 passed, 1 existing skip.
- VB workspace formatting tests: 229 passed.
- Both affected test projects built successfully with `RunAnalyzersDuringBuild=true`.
- Repository whitespace formatting verification and `git diff --check` passed.
- A 48-case probe using locally built assemblies confirmed that actual IDE0055 analysis no longer reports correctly formatted comment whitespace solely for an EOL mismatch, while genuine corrections still produce diagnostics and preferred-EOL output.

Validation ran on Windows with .NET 10. No live VS Code LSP-host or .NET Framework test run was performed. Builds reported existing package-vulnerability warnings.

Issues.Title: Add a fixall in document LSP code action
Issues.Body:
Adds support for `CodeActionParams.Context.Only` so that the server only calculates code actions for the requested kinds (Quick Fix, Refactoring, etc..). 

Also, adds support for the `source.fixAll` kind. This creates a special code action which fixes all diagnostics in the specified document. 

A `dotnet.codeAction.fixAllMinimumSeverity` option is added which filters the diagnostics to fix. The default value is set to `warning` which matches dotnet-format's default fix severity.


 ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86229)

Issues.Title: Preserve generated document query parameters through URI serialization
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Construct source-generated document URIs from logical components so they survive normal vscode-uri parsing and serialization.

The generated-document query has two distinct escaping layers: parameter values are escaped first, and the complete parameter string is then assigned as the logical URI query component. Normal URI serialization escapes that component. Deserialization reads `ParsedUri.Query` to remove the URI layer before `HttpUtility.ParseQueryString` removes the parameter-value layer.

- Add a component-based `ParsedUri.From` factory using the existing normalization, validation, and encoding implementation.
- Use it to construct source-generated document URIs without prematurely decoding parameter escapes.
- Preserve regression coverage for direct and default-client roundtrips, special characters, Unicode, and optional generator assembly paths, plus factory formatting and validation.

This supports the default URI serialization change in https://github.com/dotnet/vscode-csharp/pull/9921. No legacy-client compatibility fallback is included. Clients using `toString(true)` still work for ordinary names but are not universally compatible: values containing ampersands, plus signs, or literal percent escapes can be corrupted.

## Verification

- Before the fix, all ten new-client regression cases failed with `Could not get documentId` after normal client serialization; after the fix, they pass.
- Focused tests after removing legacy-client characterization coverage: **189 passed, 1 skipped** (existing Unix-only case on Windows):

Issues.Title: Use AntiSSRF to validate container auth realm connections
Issues.Body:
## Description

Use `Microsoft.Security.AntiSSRF` for container registry token requests. The authentication realm is the token endpoint URL supplied by the registry in its bearer authentication challenge. Its hostname is resolved and the resulting addresses are validated when a connection is opened.

Adds two environment variables to configure the address policy, including support for internal token endpoints:

### `DOTNET_CONTAINER_AUTH_REALM_POLICY`

Selects which addresses token requests may connect to.

- **`Public`** (default): Allows addresses outside the library’s private and special-use exclusions, plus any explicitly allowed addresses.
- **`AllowlistOnly`**: Allows only explicitly configured IP addresses and CIDR ranges. An empty allowlist permits no connections.
- **`None`**: Applies no address restrictions. Existing HTTP/HTTPS requirements still apply.

### `DOTNET_CONTAINER_AUTH_REALM_ALLOWED_ADDRESSES`

A semicolon-separated list of IPv4/IPv6 addresses or CIDR ranges, for example:

```text
10.20.30.40;10.50.0.0/16;fd00::/8
```

With `Public`, these entries add exceptions to the default address exclusions. With `AllowlistOnly`, they define the complete set of permitted addresses.

Issues.Title: Backport #55581 (DOTNET_HOST_PATH for in-process `dotnet run` builds) to 10.0.4xx
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

On SDK 10.0.403, `dotnet run -f net10.0-android` fails at the deploy step for an app that has a `ProjectReference` to a library whose build runs a task in a .NET task host:

```
error MSB4221: Could not run the "EmbeddedResourceInjectorTask_..." task because MSBuild could not create or connect to a task host with runtime "NET" and architecture "x64". ... Error  DOTNET_HOST_PATH is not set. Cannot determine runtime location for app host bootstrap. This should always be set when running under the .NET SDK..
Deployment to device failed. Fix any deployment errors and run again.
```

`dotnet run` builds `DeployToDevice` in its own process through `ProjectInstance.Build`, without the `DOTNET_HOST_PATH` that the forwarding app sets for `dotnet build`. `DeployToDevice` → `ResolveReferences` builds the referenced library again, and its task-host task fails. #55581 fixes exactly this ("Android ILLink targets" in its description). It's on `main` and `release/11.0.1xx`, but not on `release/10.0.4xx`.

It hits every Uno Platform app that references an Uno class library, because Uno's `EmbeddedResourceInjectorTask` is declared with `TaskFactory="TaskHostFactory" Runtime="CurrentRuntime"` in every project that references Uno.WinUI. A single-project app with only `PackageReference`s deploys fine.

### To Reproduce

1. An Android app project with a `ProjectReference` to a library project that runs a `TaskHostFactory` task during `Build` (for example, any Uno library).
2. With `DOTNET_HOST_PATH` unset in the shell, run `dotnet run -f net10.0-android` with a device attached.

Expected: deploys and starts, as `dotnet build -t:Run` does.
Actual: MSB4221 as above.

### Workarounds

- Set `DOTNET_HOST_PATH` to the `dotnet` executable in the shell.
- Set the `DOTNET_HOST_PATH` MSBuild property in the referenced library. `AssemblyTaskFactory` reads it from the project's properties.
- Use `dotnet build -f net10.0-android -t:Run`.

### Ask

Backport #55581 to the 10.0.4xx band, since .NET 10 is the LTS release, and since 10.0.300 `dotnet run` deploys mobile apps through this in-process path.

### Further technical details

- .NET SDK 10.0.403 (MSBuild 18.9.15), Android SDK pack 36.1.69, Windows 10

Issues.Title: `dotnet run app.cs` never deploys a mobile app: file-based apps skip device selection and `DeployToDevice`
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

For a file-based app that targets a device platform (`#:property TargetFramework=net10.0-android`), `dotnet run app.cs` builds the app, then tries to start it without installing it first. On Android, the run fails with only:

```
Error: Failed to start app:
```

The same app as a project (`dotnet run -f net10.0-android`) is installed and starts.

`RunCommand` creates the `RunCommandSelector`, which handles device selection and `DeployToDevice`, only when there is a project file:

```csharp
using var selector = ProjectFileFullPath is not null
    ? new RunCommandSelector(ProjectFileFullPath, ...)
    : null;
...
if (selector is not null && !selector.TryDeployToDevice()) { ... }
```

For a file-based app, `EntryPointFileFullPath` is set and `ProjectFileFullPath` is null. So `ComputeAvailableDevices` and `DeployToDevice` never run. The binlog shows one request, `Build;ComputeRunArguments;CoreCompile`, and then `RunCommand` (`dotnet exec Microsoft.Android.Run.dll ... --package <id> --activity <name>`) starts an app that isn't on the device. The code is the same on `release/10.0.4xx`, `release/11.0.1xx` and `main`.

The empty message after "Failed to start app:" is a separate problem: `Microsoft.Android.Run` doesn't pass on what `am start` reported (dotnet/android).

### To Reproduce

1. Install the `android` workload and attach a device (`adb devices` lists it).
2. Save as `app.cs` (any Android-capable SDK works. This one uses Uno.Sdk, which is where we hit it):
   ```csharp
   #:sdk Uno.Sdk@7.0.0-dev.113
   #:property TargetFramework=net10.0-android
   #:property OutputType=Exe
   #:property UnoSingleProject=true
   #:property UnoFeatures=SkiaRenderer
   // ... an app's entry point
   ```
3. Make sure the app's package isn't installed, then run `dotnet run app.cs`.

Expected: the app is installed on the device and started, and its logcat streams, as with `dotnet run -f net10.0-android` on a project.
Actual: the build succeeds, then `Error: Failed to start app:`. The package isn't installed (`adb shell pm list packages` doesn't list it).

### Workaround

Run `Install` as part of `ComputeRunArguments`, which file-based `dotnet run` does build:

```xml
<Target Name="InstallFileBasedAndroidApp"
        BeforeTargets="ComputeRunArguments"
        DependsOnTargets="Install"
        Condition="'$(FileBasedProgram)' == 'true' and '$(AndroidApplication)' == 'true'" />
```

With that, `dotnet run app.cs` installs the app, starts it and streams its logcat. The run cache also has to be turned off with `FileBasedProgramCanSkipMSBuild=false`. Otherwise, once a build is cached, the next run skips MSBuild for an unchanged file and compiles an edited one with csc alone. Then `Install` doesn't run, so an uninstalled app fails to start again and an edit never reaches the device. Device selection is still missing: with several devices attached, nothing prompts for one.

A real fix would probably also need the run cache to treat device-targeted apps as "always go through MSBuild", since a csc-only build can't package or deploy.

### Further technical details

- .NET SDK 10.0.403, Android SDK pack 36.1.69, Windows 10, Pixel 8 (Android 16)
- Not tried, but likely the same for iOS, since the `ProjectFileFullPath` check doesn't depend on the platform.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "`dotnet run app.cs` never deploys a mobile app: file-based apps skip device selection and `DeployToDevice`" (#56841)

Issues.Title: CoreGenerateSatelliteAssemblies does not forward LangVersion, causing CS8630 with unsafe-v2
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

`CoreGenerateSatelliteAssemblies` forwards `$(Features)` to its `<Csc>` task but not `$(LangVersion)`. When a project enables unsafe-v2 and specifies `LangVersion=preview`, its main compilation succeeds, but compilation of localized resource assemblies fails with CS8630.

This blocks migrating System.Text.Json and its source generators to unsafe-v2 in dotnet/runtime.

### Steps to reproduce

Create `Repro.csproj`:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>netstandard2.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>preview</LangVersion>
    <Features>$(Features);updated-memory-safety-rules</Features>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Net.Compilers.Toolset"
                      Version="5.14.0-1.26528.120"
                      PrivateAssets="all" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

The compiler package is available from the [dotnet-tools feed](https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/dnceng/public/_packaging/dotnet-tools/nuget/v3/index.json).

Add `Resources.fr.resx`:

```xml
<root>
  <data name="Message" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Bonjour</value>
  </data>
</root>
```

Run:

```console
dotnet build -c Release
```

Reproduced with SDK `12.0.100-alpha.1.26480.102`.

### Expected behavior

The build succeeds. Satellite compilation honors the project's `LangVersion=preview`.

### Actual behavior

Satellite compilation receives `/features:updated-memory-safety-rules` without `/langversion:preview`, defaults to C# 15, and fails:

```text
error CS8630: Invalid 'MemorySafetyRulesVersion' value: '2' for C# 15.0.
Please use language version 'preview' or greater.
```

### Other details

The likely fix is to forward the language version in the `<Csc>` invocation inside `CoreGenerateSatelliteAssemblies` in `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.targets`:

```xml
LangVersion="$(LangVersion)"
```

The same minimal satellite compiler invocation succeeds when `/langversion:preview` is supplied.

Issues.Title: Fix process hangs and lifetime bugs using .NET 11 APIs
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Exercise the .NET 11 Process API skill developed in dotnet/skills#1322 against real SDK code. This is a practical test of the skill's guidance on output draining, process termination versus output EOF, cancellation, handle inheritance, and resource ownership.

The changes do more than replace APIs: they fix process hangs, orphaned children, resource leaks, and an MSBuild environment-variable race, while removing substantially more code than they add.

## Bugs fixed

- **Template post-actions could deadlock on redirected output.** They waited for the child to exit before reading stdout/stderr. Drain the requested streams before waiting, reading both concurrently when both are redirected, while retaining failure diagnostics.
- **Docker image loading could deadlock on unread stdout/stderr.** Reuse the container runtime's existing streaming implementation, which drains both outputs while writing the image, closes stdin, and coordinates cancellation and child cleanup if writing fails.
- **Docker version probes could hang on full output pipes.** Discard unused output through null-device handles rather than redirecting it into unread pipes.
- **Timed-out EF script generation could leave the child running.** Modern .NET uses the run helpers' timeout cleanup; the Framework fallback explicitly kills and waits for the child.
- **The HTTPS certificate probe in `dotnet watch` could outlive timeout/cancellation.** Cancel the process operation itself, rather than only abandoning the wait, so the child is terminated and reaped.
- **EF script generation changed the parent MSBuild process's environment.** Set `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development` on the child only, avoiding interference with concurrent work in the same MSBuild process.
- **EF script completion raced with exit-event callbacks.** Replace task-wide process/exit-code/output fields with per-invocation state, read the actual exit status, and join Framework output callbacks before consuming their output. This also prevents one DbContext's output from leaking into another's diagnostics.
- **EF failures discarded captured stderr.** Report both stdout and stderr when logging is enabled.
- **Several process wrappers leaked resources or left ownership to callers.** Dispose owned processes in CLI execution/capture, formatter helpers, Docker configuration queries, and Razor shutdown; use owning run helpers where only an exit code is needed.
- **Razor shutdown blocked synchronously and ignored cancellation while waiting.** Await the termination-specific status API with the command's cancellation token.
- **Test helpers had the same output/timeout hazards.** Drain argument-reflector stdout before waiting, and capture Git output with a real timeout that cleans up the child instead of ignoring a finite wait's result.

## Additional simplifications and hardening

- Restrict incidental handle inheritance with `InheritedHandles = []` across direct launches, preserving explicitly configured inheritance where appropriate.
- Use termination-specific waits in watch, MTP, and command wrappers; keep output-reader completion separate. Remove watch/test polling workarounds for waits coupled to descendant-held output pipes.
- Replace modern Razor server startup P/Invoke and hand-escaped command lines with `StartAndForget` and argument lists. Keep Windows/.NET Framework interop and escaping out of modern compilation.
- Reduce the formatter process runner to one helper: capture stdout only when a consumer needs it, discard unused output, and own process disposal internally. Remove unused result wrappers, options, callbacks, and file-opening code.
- Use managed Unix file-mode APIs instead of spawning permission-setting/inspection subprocesses.

Modern CLI capture now preserves the original output text rather than normalizing line endings. Existing Framework-specific execution paths remain where required.

## Validation

- Focused Windows checks passed during development for template post-actions, CLI capture, formatter process/restore helpers, container probes, and EF logging, exit-code, and timeout cleanup.
- .NET Framework builds passed for Razor, CLI utilities, and publish tasks.
- `git diff --check HEAD^ HEAD` passed.

The focused checks preceded the final cleanup and review edits; they are not a claim that the final commit has had a full SDK test run. Full SDK and Unix runtime validation have not been performed.

Issues.Title: [release/11.0.1xx] Fix OpenCode environment detection
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Backport #56820 (merge commit a7d7d4460597086acc41a1cd983dcd2e361c0dc6) to `release/11.0.1xx`.

Correct the OpenCode LLM environment marker from `OPENCODE_AI` to `OPENCODE`, preserving the existing presence-based semantics: any non-empty value identifies OpenCode. Add regression cases for `OPENCODE=1`, `OPENCODE=0`, an empty value, and rejection of the incorrect `OPENCODE_AI` marker.

Original PR: https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/56820

## Upstream evidence

OpenCode's shell tool explicitly sets `invocation.env.OPENCODE = "1"` before running commands:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/77a0fd6f3b247235b09941d55ff0faf72be1dae4/packages/core/src/tool/plugin/shell.ts#L214

## Conflict resolution and branch differences

The automated backport conflicted because this branch uses static environment-detection rules that read the process environment, while main uses an injected environment-variable accessor. Only the marker correction is applied to this branch's existing rule; main's detector refactor is not included.

The regression cases use the existing MSTest `TelemetryCommonPropertiesTests` data source and save/clear/restore environment-isolation mechanism. Both `OPENCODE` and the rejected `OPENCODE_AI` marker remain in that isolation list so ambient values cannot affect the regression cases.

Main's `test/dotnet.Tests/CommandTests/Test/GivenDotnetTestOutput.cs` does not exist on this branch. No missing main-only test files or unrelated refactors are copied.

Changed files:
- `src/Cli/dotnet/Telemetry/LLMEnvironmentDetectorForTelemetry.cs`
- `test/dotnet.Tests/TelemetryTests/TelemetryCommonPropertiesTests.cs`

## Validation on this release branch

- Full Debug SDK/redist build: `build.cmd /bl:1.binlog` succeeded, 0 errors. Existing dependency-audit warnings for MessagePack and System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs remain outside this surgical backport.
- Branch test assembly and redist were built together, then `.dotnet\dotnet.exe .github\skills\targeted-test\scripts\RunTargetedTests.cs -- --project test\dotnet.Tests\dotnet.Tests.csproj --filter "FullyQualifiedName~CanDetectLLMStatusForEnvVars" --no-build` passed: **64 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped**.
- Retained local TRX: `artifacts\log\targeted-tests\dotnet.Tests\20261029-135329-42816\test-results.trx`; full build binlog: `1.binlog`.
- `git diff --check` passed.

These are release/11.0.1xx results, not main's 81-test result.

<!-- tactics-begin -->
## Tactics

### Summary

The SDK checks `OPENCODE_AI`, but OpenCode sets `OPENCODE=1` when launching commands, so its environment is not identified by the OpenCode rule. This backport replaces that marker with `OPENCODE` and retains the existing nonempty-presence semantics. It is suitable for the release branch because the production change is one environment-variable name, without main's detector refactors.

### Customer Impact

SDK commands launched through OpenCode on the affected `release/11.0.1xx` code miss the existing `opencode` LLM-environment classification unless another agent marker also matches. Ordinary non-agent invocations are unaffected. Exact affected shipped SDK versions and customer-report frequency have not been established; no customer-tested workaround is recorded. After the correction, the obsolete `OPENCODE_AI` marker alone no longer identifies OpenCode.

### Regression?

Unknown — not enough information to determine the introducing PR or first affected SDK version.

### Testing

- Updated the branch's existing MSTest data for `OPENCODE=1`, `OPENCODE=0`, empty `OPENCODE`, and rejected `OPENCODE_AI=1`; both markers are saved, cleared, and restored for isolation.
- A full local Debug SDK/redist build succeeded with zero errors.

- `git diff --check` passed. No successful branch CI result is asserted here; CI should be reviewed before merging. Main's 81-test result is separate upstream validation.

### Risk

Low. Only the OpenCode marker changes in production; other agent rules and matching semantics remain unchanged. The two-file backport includes regression coverage for nonempty, empty, and obsolete markers and avoids unrelated main-branch changes.

Issues.Title: Roll bundled web templates forward to .NET 12
Issues.Body:
## Summary

- Bundle the flowing, unsuffixed `Microsoft.DotNet.Web.ItemTemplates`, `Microsoft.DotNet.Web.ProjectTemplates`, and `Microsoft.McpServer.ProjectTemplates` packages instead of manually pinned `.11.0` packages. Web/Blazor/Worker/MCP scaffolding now defaults to and accepts `net12.0`.
- Restore `TemplateFrameworkVersion` to `$(MajorMinorVersion)`. This is an installer-group identity: the web project package determines the install path and MSI component version. Advancing the group keeps SDK/MSI staging and latest-MSI selection aligned; it does not retarget common template contents. Common package identities/content and desktop package wiring are unchanged.
- Update existing end-to-end default-framework expectations and the three web help snapshots for the .NET 12 web templates.
- Adjust existing installation tests and approvals for the newly bundled package identity, and extend supported-version data and dependent roll-forward cases to .NET 12.

This is independent of #56404 and does not include its common-template content, identity, or localization changes.

Thanks to @dsplaisted for the [starting-point suggestion](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/55851#issuecomment-6424262124).

Changelog

Sourced from becheran/mlc's changelog.

Changelog

[Unreleased] - ReleaseDate

[1.3.0] - 2026-10-20

Added

  • --quiet / -q option (and quiet in .mlc.toml) which only prints warnings, errors and the summary. The banner and all links which are ok or skipped are left out
  • --format json option (and format = "json" in .mlc.toml) which prints a single JSON document with the summary and all issues to stdout. Debug output goes to stderr in this mode
  • Documentation for AI agents and automation: README section, AGENTS.md, llms.txt and ready to copy examples for AGENTS.md, Claude Code hooks and skills, and pre-commit

Changed

  • Rust edition 2024. Building from source needs Rust 1.88 or newer, which is checked in CI
  • Invalid arguments (for example --throttle abc or an unknown markup type) and an invalid .mlc.toml print an error and exit with code 2 instead of panicking. The same exit code is used for an invalid --root-dir, which used to be 1
  • Failing to write the --csv file prints an error instead of panicking. A web link which is not a valid URL is reported as broken link instead of panicking
  • The banner is not printed anymore when --help or an invalid argument is passed
  • Warnings about not existing paths passed via --files or --ignore-path are printed to stderr instead of stdout
  • The CSV report and the list of broken links are sorted (errors first, then by file, line and column) instead of depending on which web request finished first
  • Library: mlc::run returns Result<(), mlc::Error>, the Display implementation of Config, the glob re-export of colored and the async-ness of link_validator::resolve_target_link are gone, logger::init takes a second use_stderr argument and MarkupType::file_extensions returns a slice
  • The release binary is much smaller (release profile with LTO, opt-level = "s", panic = "abort" and stripped symbols, and the unused code above). This means faster downloads in CI and a faster start
  • The docker image is based on Alpine Linux instead of Ubuntu and is about 10 times smaller. The entrypoint.sh of the GitHub Action uses sh instead of bash

Fixed

  • gitignore = false and gituntracked = false in .mlc.toml enabled the options. Now they are only enabled with true
  • --gitignore and --gituntracked now also recognize the markup files with extensions like .markdown or .htm and upper case extensions

Removed

  • Dependencies lazy_static and async-std. The standard library is used instead
  • The second, never used TLS implementation (rustls with aws-lc) and the response decoders (brotli, gzip, deflate) and charset detection of reqwest. They were compiled in, but the web links are checked with the system TLS library and only the status code of a response is looked at. The Accept-Encoding header is still sent

Issues.Title: Add weekly CLI agent detection evidence audit
Issues.Body:
Coding agents change, and the CLI's checks for recognizing them can go stale. This PR adds a weekly audit that checks those signals against current upstream source and documentation, looks for popular agents we might be missing, and keeps the results in one tracking issue.

When the audit finds a missing environment variable for an agent we already recognize, a separate workflow can investigate it and open a tested **draft PR**. The goal is to catch detection gaps and bring small fixes to a maintainer—not approve or merge changes automatically. Findings that need broader changes stay in the report.

### Examples

- The [audit found OpenCode's `OPENCODE=1` signal](https://github.com/baronfel/sdk-llm-detection-trial-20261028/actions/runs/40799598457) without being told the variable or where to find it. The SDK currently checks `OPENCODE_AI`.
- The [fixer then built the patched SDK, passed all 65 telemetry cases, and opened a signed draft PR](https://github.com/baronfel/sdk-llm-detection-trial-20261028/actions/runs/40813026553): [baronfel/sdk-llm-detection-trial-20261028#3](https://github.com/baronfel/sdk-llm-detection-trial-20261028/pull/3). It preserves the old variable and adds the new one with four regression cases.
- The [closed-tracker check](https://github.com/baronfel/sdk-llm-detection-trial-20261028/actions/runs/40795210491) confirmed that closing the issue stops report updates without creating another issue.

The audit and manually dispatched fixer ran successfully; the new automatic handoff between them has not yet been exercised in a hosted run.

<details>
<summary>Implementation and validation details</summary>

### How it works

- The audit runs weekly or on demand. It researches existing detection rules and up to five missing harnesses. It reports uncertainty rather than treating missing evidence as proof.
- A separate dispatcher reads structured findings after a successful main-branch audit and starts at most one fixer. The audit agent gains no new permissions.
- The fixer can only add one harness-prefixed variable to an existing presence-based rule, plus four generated test rows. It cannot remove legacy signals, change matching rules, or add agent labels.
- A separate job builds the patched SDK and runs the telemetry matrix without publishing credentials. Threat detection, exact-content checks, and a patch/metadata digest must pass before draft publication.
- Closing the tracker or leaving a fix PR open stops new automatic proposals. Previously attempted or rejected aliases are skipped; maintainers can retry manually.

The trusted patch limit remains 16 KiB across exactly two C# files. Signed publication has a separate 32 KiB budget because it sends complete file contents.

### Validation and limits

All **107 Node tests** passed, including real Git patch and publication-CLI tests, candidate validation, duplicate/retry controls, and mocked dispatcher API calls. Strict workflow compilation, actionlint, compiled permission/gate checks, and 202 local documentation links also passed.

The hosted trials used their own credential and a full SDK checkout pinned to `7d24d6cf305b1d175811c32490bdd3d543ad51c1`. Production PAT-pool authentication and installed agent runtime behavior remain untested. The audit is source-based, not a live harness test.

The automatic handoff activates after merge. This PR changes workflow tooling, not the production detector; the example OpenCode change exists only in the private draft PR.

</details>

Issues.Body:
On October 25, 2026, we released out-of-band security updates for .NET 8.0.33, .NET 9.0.22, .NET 10.0.14, and .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 (prerelease). We recommend updating affected applications and build environments as soon as possible. .NET Framework is not affected.

The October 13 updates did not fully address CVE-2026-70197 and CVE-2026-102870. These out-of-band updates provide the corrected fixes; the original advisory identities and revision history are preserved. For CVE-2026-102870, update the affected standalone Server/DevServer package references; updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute.

Update those inputs and recreate their extracted workspaces using ownership-controlled extraction; review and rebuild affected downstream outputs as needed. .NET 10/11 applicability is limited to source-built distributions.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-114148 | .NET Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-114148](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-114148) ### Acknowledgements - Alen Cheung ### Revisions V1.0 (10/25/2026): Initial advisory.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 | .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages
